I almost fell for a suspicious job opportunity just because I’m job hunting. 😅

I had just finished applying for a job when I received an email from a “recruiter” almost immediately.

I opened the email with excitement and that little rush of adrenaline you get when you think, “Wait… did someone actually notice me?” 😂

Then I saw the offer:
$70,000–$95,000+ per year for a Lead Executive Virtual Assistant role.

I didn’t apply for this particular role, so I was curious.

The email explained the role, listed responsibilities, and even explained why my background was a good fit.

But then I got to the end of the email and saw this:
“Thanks for sharing your journey. I hope you find the right opportunity soon. If you'd like to discuss career positioning or share ideas about your job search, I'd be glad to connect.”

Wait… what? 😂

That didn’t quite match the rest of the email.

So, instead of getting carried away by the salary, I copied the entire email and sent it to my almighty assistant, Claude AI. 😂

I asked it to explain the email to me like I was 5 years old and help me identify anything suspicious.

And honestly, that was a good decision.

It helped me come up with questions I should ask before sharing my CV:
• Who is the hiring company?
• Who exactly is the recruiter?
• Can I verify the recruiter professionally?
• What is the actual employment/contract structure?
• What are the working hours and time zone?
• What is the exact scope of the role?

I asked.

The recruiter said the company couldn't be disclosed until I was shortlisted and asked me to send my CV.

I then asked for the recruiter's LinkedIn profile.

The response?

“My corporate LinkedIn network portal is currently undergoing an official platform restructuring and security migration…”

Hmm. 😂And here's where it got more interesting: the email addresses kept changing- Gmail, then a company domain, and now another Gmail address.
At that point, I decided not to share my CV until the recruiter and firm could be independently verified.

So basically, every time I asked for something I could use to verify the opportunity, I got a reason why I couldn't verify it.

And that experience reminded me of something important:
Job seekers are vulnerable too.

When you're actively looking for work, an unexpected offer, especially one with an attractive salary, can make you want to move quickly.

But please, don't let excitement make you skip your due diligence.

Before sending your CV or personal information to an unfamiliar recruiter:

-Verify the recruiter
-Check the company
-Ask questions about the role
-Be cautious when information is deliberately vague
-Don't allow an attractive salary to rush your decision
-Never send sensitive personal or financial information to an unverified contact

Sometimes, the best response to a great-looking opportunity isn't “How quickly can I apply?”
It's “Let me verify this first.”

AI Governance: Regulators Now Want Proof, Not Promises

Colorado has an AI law now. New York has one covering AI used in hiring. More states are adding their own every few months. Over 60% of businesses will be required to have a formal AI governance framework this year, according to Gartner. Regulators used to just ask businesses to be careful. Now they’re asking for proof, and most businesses don’t have any.

Here’s how that gap happened. Over the last couple years, businesses rolled out AI fast, chatbots, hiring tools, automated decisions, without writing any of it down. Nobody tracked which tools were in use, what they were actually doing, or who was checking the AI’s decisions before they affected a real person. That was fine when nobody asked. Now someone is asking, and “we’ve just been using it” isn’t going to hold up.

Governance just means having an answer ready. What AI tools are actually running in the business. What each one is used for, and how much risk that use carries. And proof that an actual person reviews anything the AI decides that touches hiring, customers, or sensitive information.

The cost of skipping this isn’t abstract anymore. It’s fines under laws that already exist. And increasingly, it’s clients who won’t sign a contract until you can show them this is handled. In some industries, having this documented isn’t optional anymore, it’s the price of doing business.

This isn’t about using less AI. It’s about being able to show someone, in writing, that a person is actually watching how it gets used.

It requires perhaps less structure than we tend to think, and  being much more intentional about workplace design to unlock what is clearly immense, underutilised potential. 🤔🤝

The organisations that will attract the best  talent tomorrow will be those that embrace transparency, leverage AI ethically, design for neuroinclusion, and adapt to the fluid reality of future and modern employment. 7 Direct Threats to the Indian BPO Industry

The Indian BPO industry is entering a phase where traditional cost and manpower advantages may no longer be enough.

1. AI & Automation replacing traditional BPO processes
Impact: Lower headcount requirements, reduced transaction-based billing, and pressure on traditional outsourcing models.

2. Global economic slowdown & cautious client spending
Impact: Lower revenues, delayed expansion, hiring freezes, pricing pressure, and margin compression.

3. Geopolitical conflicts & global trade disruptions
Impact: Cost escalation, currency volatility, delayed client decisions, and business-continuity risks.

4. Cybersecurity threats & customer data breaches
Impact: Financial penalties, higher compliance costs, reputational damage, and potential client attrition.

5. Competition from GCCs & alternative outsourcing destinations
Impact: Greater competition for deals, pricing pressure, and the need to demonstrate measurable business value beyond labor arbitrage.

6. Rising operating costs & shrinking margins
Impact: Greater productivity pressure, workforce optimization, site consolidation, and difficult cost decisions.

7. Stricter client expectations & evolving quality models
Impact: Higher service-level expectations, contract penalties, increased rework, and potential loss of business.

My perspective on the biggest structural change

The biggest long-term challenge may not be a global recession or geopolitical conflict.

It is the transformation from a manpower-based outsourcing model to a technology-enabled, outcome-based service model.

For BPO leaders, the future will require more than people management. It will require strong capabilities in:

• Operational excellence
• Process redesign
• AI & automation governance
• Quality analytics
• Digital transformation
• Outcome-based delivery

The question is no longer simply: “How efficiently can we manage people?”

It is increasingly becoming:

“How effectively can we combine people, technology and intelligence to deliver measurable business outcomes?”

That shift could define the next phase of the Indian BPO industry.

I think a lot of people in software are going through some version of this.

Your contract expires, or you get laid off, and when you start looking for the next job you realize the industry you knew has changed underneath you. All the time you spent learning the technology and business around your previous work suddenly feels less valuable. You wonder whether you should have spent more of that time on AI, because now AI seems to be becoming a requirement for staying employable.

Maybe you have been programming for decades. You have seen technologies come and go before, but this feels different. You are also older now, and while you see decades of experience, some hiring managers may see someone who could be resistant to change.

So you keep applying, but at the same time you dive as deeply into AI as you can. Not because it is just another interesting technology to learn, but because this time it feels existential. I know this because I am living some version of it right now.

You start projects, experiment, and look for problems other people may have missed. Partly because you want to learn, partly because you want to prove that you can still build something relevant, and partly because after working for most of your adult life you have forgotten how not to work. The empty space is uncomfortable. Working on technical problems gives you purpose and keeps the bigger worries quiet for a while.

Your family believes in you, but sometimes you can see the worry creeping in. You talk about ideas, architectures, models, agents, research, things you would normally discuss with colleagues. They listen because they care about you, even when much of what you are saying is difficult to follow. And you realize they are carrying some of this uncertainty too.

You worry about the next job, where the industry is going, and whether the projects you are putting so much energy into will become some of the countless projects that never get finished, never get used, or never get noticed. So you put that worry back into the work and keep going. When other people depend on you, giving up does not feel like an option.

Then you open LinkedIn and realize everyone seems to be processing the same uncertainty in public. AI adoption is too fast. AI adoption is too slow. AI will replace us. AI will make us more productive. Coding is dead. Coding has never been more exciting. Everyone wants confirmation that they understood what is happening correctly.

I am not sure anyone really knows yet.

We are living through a very strange transition in software. There is enormous opportunity, but also enormous uncertainty, and behind all these arguments are real people trying to figure out whether they still have a place in the industry while their families quietly live through that uncertainty with them.

It is a strange time. Be kind.

An 89% union vote in Calgary. A bipartisan letter to the FCC. And 10,000 new contact center jobs in Metro Manila.

All in the same week.

WestJet's Calgary contact center staff voted 89% to join Unifor — two years after roughly 400 of their colleagues' roles moved to agents in El Salvador. Days later, a Democrat from Arizona and a Republican from West Virginia co-signed a letter asking the FCC to force call centers to disclose which country an agent is sitting in, plus guarantee callers a right to reach a human when AI is running the call.

Don't read this as a threat to Philippine outsourcing. Read it as a change in the rules of the game.

The work isn't disappearing. TP is hiring for 10,000+ roles across Mega Manila right now — telecom, healthcare, financial services, travel. 60,000 employees here after 30 years.

The work is relocating. And the politics is a response to the direction of travel, not the volume.

What actually shifts for anyone running delivery here:

Offshoring just stopped being purely an economics story and became an organized one. A unionized client-side center means the next transition gets negotiated differently — slower, more publicly, with a press release written by someone who isn't you.

Country disclosure, if it passes, turns delivery location from a contractual line item into a consumer-facing fact. Buyers will start asking how you handle that. The smart ones already are.

Then there's the quiet part. Novo Nordisk cut 13,000 roles in a year — and 4,000 of those never showed up in a restructuring announcement at all. They just didn't replace people. Most headcount leaves a large employer this way, invisible to every layoff tracker. The displacement numbers everyone quotes are understating real movement.

Meanwhile, four in 10 workers now believe quitting and rejoining beats staying for a raise — up from 18% two years ago. And U.S. job openings, hires, quits and layoffs are all flat.

Nobody's moving. When exit stops working, voice is what's left. That's the thread connecting all of it.

The Philippines isn't watching this from the sidelines. It's the market these policies are being written about. The providers who treat country disclosure, workforce stability, and retention economics as operational problems to solve — not PR problems to manage — will be the ones still winning contracts in 2027.

The rest will be reacting to someone else's press release.

1. long contracts hide bad work.

2. the buyers we work with, heads of growth and marketing at real estate and finance companies, won't sign anything longer anyway. Fighting that wastes everyone's time

3. a plan the client owns gets executed. A plan that only lives in an agency's deck gets forgotten the day the retainer ends

The downside is obvious. 

Revenue is less predictable, and I've had clients use the 30-day out. However, most of them stick around. Our typical engagement has run 9 months or more, because the work has to hold up every month.

If you're hiring an agency and they won't let you buy the strategy on its own, ask what they're worried you'll find out.
